items.title: Explained: What Keralam’s new Senior Citizens’ Rights Bill covers
items.summary: The Keralam Assembly, on October 26, unanimously passed the Keralam Senior Citizens’ (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, which seeks to establish a legal framework for protecting the rights, dignity and social security of people aged 60 and above. The Bill provides for the registration, regulation and monitoring of senior citizen care centres, caregiver training and certification, and measures to prevent abuse and exploitation of the elderly. It also seeks to promote healthy and active ageing and ensure support to families and caregivers. The Bill also proposes dedicated protection units at the state and district levels, a public register of certified caregivers, specialised cyber cells to address fraud targeting senior citizens, a State Reserve Fund for their welfare, and penalties for offences including abuse, abandonment and the illegal possession of an elderly resident’s property. The legislation had been referred to the Finance Subject Committee for scrutiny before being taken up in the Assembly. items.title: One bite at the cherry: Henderson comes to India and finds it was already here
items.summary: Every judge recognises a certain kind of litigant. He loses on one ground and, after judgment, discovers another. When that fails, he changes the forum, recasts the relief, or presents an old controversy as a new cause of action. Litigation becomes less a means of resolving a dispute than a means of keeping it alive. The law calls this abuse of process. In Henderson v Henderson (1843) , Sir James Wigram V-C articulated a principle later developed into a broader inquiry into successive proceedings: parties should ordinarily advance matters which, exercising reasonable diligence, ought to have been raised earlier. This does not mean every omitted argument is lost forever. The question is whether a later proceeding unfairly reopens a controversy that ought to have ended. Finality is indispensable to justice, but must not defeat a genuine claim. India already has safeguards Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908 embodies constructive res judicata . A matter which might and ought to have been raised as a ground of attack or defence in the former suit is deemed to have been directly and substantially in issue. Order II Rule 2 CPC addresses omitted claims

The Court said that guidelines alone will not be sufficient to tackle the menace, and enforcement accountability of concerned officers would be the key. The decision was taken at a meeting of the Collegium held on October 26, 2026. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media. This will change the whole concept of news. If I am left to the mercy of the data principal on whether he or she will give consent, the concept of news will be gone... News has to be new. It will close down the newsroom. What’s the point if I have to ask for permission and consent?” said Senior Advocate Madhavi Divan, representing the digital wings of 21 mainstream news outlets, according to LiveLaw . Others raised similar concerns before. When the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on November 15 last year, the DIGIPUB News India Foundation said the Act and the Rules “endanger source confidentiality, hinder public-interest investigations, obstruct anti-corruption disclosures”. "The State Police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation...Six years have been erased from the life of a man on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures. Not even a rudimentary investigation was carried out...The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means bring in a conviction," the Bench remarked. It observed that the botched investigation put an innocent citizen’s life and liberty into serious jeopardy. "This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty...We were appalled at the manner in which the investigation was carried out," the Bench noted. State of UP] . A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana reviewed the progress of the ongoing trial and emphasised that the prosecution must strike a balance between timely disposal and fair procedure. "Your duty is to ensure that your witnesses are present. Let the trial be timely concluded. We do not want such a hurry that witnesses, cross-examinations or material evidence are left out. During the hearing, the Additional Advocate General for Uttar Pradesh informed the Bench that a special public prosecutor had been appointed to steer the trial, adding that 90 out of 131 prosecution witnesses had already been examined, leaving around 41 witnesses. items.title: Preaching religion without prior permission can lead to cancellation of OCI registration: Madras High Court
items.summary: The Madras High Court recently held that preaching one's religion without prior permission from the Central government is sufficient grounds for cancelling a foreign national's Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) registration, even if no religious conversions take place [John Daniel Vs UOI] Justice D Bharatha Chakravarthy observed that missionary activities are not limited to religious conversions and that OCI cardholders are required to obtain prior permission even to preach or spread their religion. items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently declined to quash criminal proceedings against a 22-year-old man accused of sending emails with threats of bomb blasts at Kempegowda International Airport and several shopping malls in Bengaluru [ Abhay Shee v. State of Karnataka ]. The accused youth is alleged to have impersonated another person and invoked the name of the banned terrorist organisation Jaish-e-Mohammed in the bomb threat emails. Justice M Nagaprasanna The case arose from an email allegedly sent to the Bengaluru City Police Commissioner's office on November 30, 2025, threatening explosions at the airport and malls, including Orion Mall, Lulu Mall, Forum South Mall and Mantri Square Mall.
